_note: Adult oral maxima taken from FDA product labelling. These are general labelled ceilings for a typical adult, NOT personalised limits: a prescriber may legitimately go above or (more often) far below them. MediGraph AI only compares arithmetic against these numbers and always refers the result back to a clinician.

acetaminophen.note: Many sources advise 3000 mg/day or less for regular use, and lower in liver disease, low body weight or regular alcohol use. Remember combination cold and pain products also contain it.
acetaminophen.source_name: FDA Drug Safety Communication on acetaminophen (prescription combination products)

ibuprofen.note: Over-the-counter self-treatment is capped at 1200 mg/day. Doses above that are prescription-only and are kept as short as possible.
ibuprofen.source_name: FDA label for ibuprofen (Dosage and Administration)

naproxen.note: Over-the-counter use is capped at 660 mg/day.
naproxen.source_name: FDA label for naproxen (Dosage and Administration)

aspirin.note: Low-dose aspirin for clot prevention is usually 75-100 mg daily; higher analgesic doses are a different use.

amoxicillin.note: Typical adult dosing is 500 mg three times daily or 875 mg twice daily; higher totals are used for some infections.
amoxicillin.source_name: FDA label for amoxicillin (Dosage and Administration)

metformin.note: Extended-release products are capped at 2000 mg/day. Lower limits apply with reduced kidney function.
metformin.source_name: FDA label for metformin hydrochloride (Dosage and Administration)

tramadol.note: 300 mg/day is the maximum from age 75, and lower limits apply in kidney or liver impairment.
tramadol.source_name: FDA label for tramadol hydrochloride (Dosage and Administration)

sertraline.source_name: FDA label for sertraline (Dosage and Administration)

escitalopram.note: 10 mg/day is the recommended maximum for people over 60 and in liver impairment.

simvastatin.note: 80 mg is restricted to people already tolerating it for 12 months, and lower caps apply with amlodipine, verapamil or diltiazem.
simvastatin.source_name: FDA label for simvastatin (Dosage and Administration)

prednisone.note: Doses are highly condition-specific and are often far higher for short bursts; this figure is a common upper maintenance dose only.

prednisolone.note: As with prednisone, short high-dose courses are common and legitimate.

omeprazole.note: Higher doses are used for specific conditions such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

cetirizine.note: 5 mg/day in significant kidney or liver impairment and in older adults.

azithromycin.note: A 1 g single dose is used for some specific infections.

levothyroxine.note: Doses are individually titrated by blood tests and are usually written in micrograms (300 mcg = 0.3 mg).

alprazolam.note: Lower maxima apply in older adults and with liver impairment.

gabapentin.note: Dose is reduced according to kidney function.

ondansetron.note: Single intravenous doses above 16 mg are avoided because of QT prolongation.

warfarin.note: Warfarin has no fixed maximum: the dose is set entirely by INR blood tests, so this figure is only a sanity check on typical maintenance dosing.

furosemide.note: Most outpatients take far less; high doses are reserved for resistant oedema.

spironolactone.note: Heart-failure dosing is usually 12.5-50 mg daily.

acetaminophen.note: Commonly 10-15 mg/kg per dose, up to 5 doses in 24 hours, not exceeding the adult maximum.

ibuprofen.note: Commonly 5-10 mg/kg per dose every 6-8 hours, not exceeding the adult maximum.

amoxicillin.note: Typically 25-45 mg/kg/day, and up to 80-90 mg/kg/day for ear infections.
